headings.title: Introduction and Overview of Ebola Virus Disease
headings.content: Ebola Virus Disease (EVD), formerly known as Ebola haemorrhagic fever, is a severe, often fatal illness in humans caused by the Ebola virus. As an emerging public health threat in sub-Saharan Africa, understanding EVD is crucial for nursing students in Nigeria and across the continent. The virus belongs to the Filoviridae family and is a zoonotic pathogen, meaning it naturally circulates in animal reservoirs, particularly fruit bats, before spilling over into the human population. Outbreaks typically occur in remote villages in Central and West Africa, near tropical rainforests, but can rapidly spread to densely populated urban environments if public health measures are delayed. For nursing professionals, recognizing the historical context, epidemiological patterns, and global health implications of EVD is the first line of defense. Nurses must remain vigilant, educated, and culturally competent to address community fears, stigma, and misconceptions surrounding the disease. Education remains a powerful tool in demystifying the virus and ensuring prompt reporting of suspected cases to local health authorities, ultimately mitigating outbreak severity before it overwhelms fragile healthcare infrastructures.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Transmission Dynamics
headings.content: The pathophysiology of Ebola Virus Disease is characterized by severe immune evasion, systemic inflammation, and profound coagulopathy. Once introduced into the human body via mucous membranes, breaks in the skin, or parenteral routes, the virus primarily targets endothelial cells, mononuclear phagocytes, and hepatocytes. It triggers a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, often referred to as a 'cytokine storm,' leading to systemic shock, multi-organ dysfunction, and increased vascular permeability. This vascular leakage accounts for the characteristic hypovolemic shock and internal fluid shifts seen in advanced cases. Furthermore, the virus disrupts the clotting cascade, resulting in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which manifests as bleeding from puncture sites, mucosal surfaces, and the gastrointestinal tract. Transmission dynamics dictate that the virus does not spread through casual contact or airborne routes; rather, transmission occurs strictly through direct contact—via broken skin or mucous membranes—with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected people, as well as with surfaces and materials contaminated with these fluids. Traditional burial practices involving direct contact with deceased bodies also play a significant historical role in amplifying transmission during outbreaks.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Staging
headings.content: The clinical presentation of Ebola Virus Disease evolves through distinct stages, typically following an incubation period of 2 to 21 days. The early stage (dry phase) is non-specific and mimics many other tropical infections like malaria, typhoid, or Lassa fever. Symptoms include sudden onset of high fever, severe fatigue, intense headache, muscle pain (myalgia), and arthralgia. As the disease progresses to the gastrointestinal stage (wet phase), patients develop profuse, watery diarrhea, severe nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, which rapidly precipitates severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalances. In the severe or late stage, hemorrhagic manifestations may occur—such as petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, and bleeding from venipuncture sites—though frank hemorrhage is not universal. Neurological symptoms like confusion, encephalopathy, and coma can also emerge. Patients either succumb to multi-organ failure, severe hypotension, and shock within 7 to 14 days of symptom onset, or they begin a slow convalescence if their immune system mounts an effective neutralizing antibody response. Staging is vital for nurses to anticipate clinical deterioration and tailor supportive interventions promptly.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Diagnosis
headings.content: Nursing assessment and diagnosis of Ebola Virus Disease require a high index of suspicion, rigorous adherence to infection control, and rapid clinical evaluation. Nurses in primary health settings must perform thorough epidemiological triage, screening patients immediately for travel history to outbreak areas, contact with confirmed EVD cases, or participation in high-risk funeral rites. Assessment focuses on vital signs—monitoring for hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnea—as well as quantifying fluid loss from vomiting and diarrhea. Nursing diagnoses commonly include Deficient Fluid Volume, Risk for Imbalanced Electrolyte, Acute Pain, and Risk for Infection Transmission. Laboratory confirmation is essential for a definitive diagnosis and is typically achieved via Reverse Transcription-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) assay on blood specimens. However, because lab results may take time and the disease progresses rapidly, nurses must initiate isolation and standard barrier nursing precautions based on clinical presentation and epidemiological risk factors rather than waiting for lab confirmation. Documenting intake and output accurately is critical, although challenging due to the risk of contaminating recording sheets; specialized charting protocols should be utilized outside the isolation perimeter.

headings.title: Primary Health Care Management and Supportive Treatment
headings.content: Primary health care management of Ebola Virus Disease focuses heavily on aggressive supportive therapy, symptom alleviation, and hemodynamic stabilization, as there is no single universally curative drug, though specific monoclonal antibodies have shown remarkable efficacy. Nursing management centers on rigorous fluid resuscitation using oral rehydration therapy (ORT) for mild cases and intravenous (IV) fluid replacement with balanced crystalloids (such as Ringer's lactate) for severe dehydration caused by vomiting and diarrhea. Electrolyte imbalances, particularly hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and hypocalcemia, must be aggressively corrected based on laboratory parameters. Symptomatic treatment includes administering antipyretics (such as paracetamol) for high fever while avoiding non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or aspirin due to their bleeding risks. Antiemetics, antidiarrheals, and nutritional support via enteral feeding or parenteral routes are vital components of care. Furthermore, nurses monitor for secondary bacterial infections and administer prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics and antimalarials, given that malaria shares clinical features with early EVD and is endemic in Nigeria. Psychological support and compassionate care are equally essential to reassure patients and their families.

headings.title: Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) in Primary Health Settings
headings.content: Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) is the cornerstone of halting Ebola outbreaks in primary health settings. Nurses must strictly adhere to standard, contact, and droplet precautions when interacting with any suspected or confirmed patient. Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) must be donned and doffed meticulously under the supervision of a trained observer (buddy system) to prevent self-contamination. PPE ensembles typically include impermeable gowns, heavy-duty gloves, face shields or goggles, respiratory protection (N95 or equivalent), and boot covers. Hand hygiene using alcohol-based hand rub or soap and water must be performed consistently. Environmental hygiene is equally critical; all surfaces, patient care equipment, and floors must be decontaminated using a freshly prepared chlorine solution (e.g., 0.5% for surfaces, 0.05% for handwashing). Safe handling and disposal of infectious waste, including sharps and contaminated linens, must follow strict institutional protocols. Furthermore, safe and dignified burial management must be enforced in communities, led by trained burial teams, to eliminate exposure risks from deceased individuals who remain highly infectious post-mortem.

headings.title: Community Surveillance, Contact Tracing, and Public Health Response
headings.content: Community surveillance, contact tracing, and a robust public health response are indispensable for containing EVD outbreaks at the grass-roots level. Nurses frequently serve as frontline public health officers who educate communities, dispel rumors, and encourage active participation in disease surveillance. Contact tracing involves identifying every person who has had contact with an infected individual within 21 days of symptom onset. These contacts must be monitored daily for fever and other EVD symptoms for a full 21-day incubation period from their last date of exposure. Prompt identification of a symptomatic contact allows for immediate quarantine and early clinical care, drastically altering survival outcomes and stopping transmission chains. Public health response also relies heavily on community engagement and culturally sensitive communication, working closely with local leaders, traditional healers, and youth groups to foster trust. Nurses must address social stigma, as fear of isolation or community ostracization often drives patients to hide their illness or seek care from traditional providers, inadvertently amplifying the spread of the virus within households and neighborhoods.

headings.title: Complications, Survivorship, and Post-Ebola Syndrome
headings.content: As therapeutic advancements improve survival rates, nursing care must increasingly focus on complications, survivorship, and Post-Ebola Syndrome (PES). Survivors often experience a constellation of chronic physical and psychological sequelae collectively known as Post-Ebola Syndrome. Common manifestations include chronic fatigue, arthralgia (joint pain), myalgia, headaches, ocular complications such as uveitis (which can lead to blindness), and hearing loss. Psychologically, survivors frequently face depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and severe social stigma from their communities. Furthermore, nurses must counsel survivors regarding viral persistence; the Ebola virus can persist in immunologically privileged sites—such as the semen, intraocular fluid, and central nervous system—for months after recovery. Male survivors, in particular, must be educated on safe sex practices and provided with condoms or semen testing to prevent sexual transmission of the virus. Comprehensive multidisciplinary rehabilitation programs, including physical therapy, psychological counseling, and peer support groups, are vital components of holistic nursing care to help survivors reintegrate safely into society and reclaim their health.
